claims.text: The initial HfNbTaTiZr alloy is a single-phase BCC solid solution with a random atomic distribution and no significant SRO.
Percolation of chemical SRO clusters in a single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy produces a non-monotonic transition in thermal conductivity.
Before percolation, isolated SRO clusters or associated point defects decrease thermal conductivity through increased phonon scattering.
Once SRO clusters form a connected network, thermal conductivity increases or remains anomalously high.
A connected SRO network suppresses phonon scattering by creating coherent vibrational pathways.
Standard serial and parallel mixing models do not capture the proposed percolation-mediated conductivity mechanism.
Oxygen and carbon impurities stabilize the alpha-HCP phase, increase the alpha-to-beta transition temperature, and can prevent formation of single beta-BCC HfNbTaTiZr without extreme quenching.
Annealing below the secondary-phase solvus but above the SRO diffusion threshold will nucleate and grow SRO clusters to percolation, while rapid quenching will freeze that SRO state.
The relevant transport regime occurs when the phonon mean free path is comparable to the SRO cluster correlation length.
Percolating SRO changes the local potential-energy surface so that its phonon-scattering cross-section is lower than that of isolated SRO clusters.
Percolating SRO modifies the global vibrational density of states and reduces the effective disorder potential.
The reduced disorder potential lowers the phonon-scattering rate or increases phonon group velocity.
Standard interatomic potentials often fail to capture the dynamic coupling between SRO evolution and phonons.
Thermal conductivity reaches a minimum just before the SRO network percolates and then increases after percolation.
The magnitude of the conductivity increase correlates with SRO-network connectivity rather than SRO volume fraction alone.
Simple point-defect scattering and serial or parallel mixing models predict a monotonic decrease in conductivity as SRO volume fraction increases.
The proposed effect requires SRO percolation without a B2 or L21 transformation or secondary-phase precipitation.
The effect disappears when SRO clusters remain too small or isolated to percolate, or when temperature is too high for SRO to persist.
The exact percolation threshold and conductivity increase depend on the interatomic potential used to model SRO evolution.
Oxygen impurities introduce variability by affecting both BCC phase stability and SRO formation.
